content: In mathematics, a matrix is a rectangular array of elements, which can be numbers or more abstract quantities that can be added and multiplied. Matrices are used to represent linear equations, track coefficients of linear transformations, and store data dependent on multiple parameters. The study of matrices is a part of matrix theory, and they are fundamental in linear algebra. Matrices can be added, multiplied, and decomposed in various ways. The entries of a matrix are typically real or complex numbers unless otherwise specified. The horizontal lines in a matrix are called rows, and the vertical lines are called columns. A matrix with (m) rows and (n) columns is referred to as an (m times n) matrix, where (m) and (n) are its dimensions. The dimensions are always stated with the number of rows first, followed by the number of columns. Two matrices of the same dimensions are considered equal if their corresponding entries are identical. The entry located in the (i)-th row and (j)-th column of a matrix is referred to as the ((i, j))-th entry. Rows are always listed before columns. Matrices are usually denoted by uppercase letters, while their entries are represented by the corresponding lowercase letters with subscripts. For example, the ((i, j))-th entry of a matrix (A) is commonly written as (a_{i,j}). Some authors use boldface uppercase letters to distinguish matrices from other variables. A matrix where one of the dimensions equals one is often called a vector. An (m times 1) matrix is called a column vector, while a (1 times n) matrix is called a row vector. Mathematical Definition An (m times n) matrix (A) is a function that maps the Cartesian product of the sets ({1, 2, ldots, m}) and ({1, 2, ldots, n}) to a set (S), where (S) is any non-empty set. If matrix algebra is to be defined, (S) must be a ring, and (A) must be a square matrix. The set of all square matrices over a ring forms a ring itself, often referred to as a matrix ring. Basic Operations 1. Addition: Two matrices of identical dimensions can be added by summing their corresponding entries. 2. Scalar Multiplication: A matrix can be multiplied by a scalar by multiplying each entry of the matrix by the scalar. 3. Matrix Multiplication: The product of two matrices (A) and (B) is defined only if the number of columns in (A) equals the number of rows in (B). The resulting matrix has dimensions determined by the rows of (A) and the columns of (B). Matrix multiplication is associative and distributive but not commutative. Linear Transformations Matrices can represent linear transformations between finite-dimensional vector spaces. For a linear map (f: mathbb{R}^n to mathbb{R}^m), there exists a unique (m times n) matrix (A) such that (f(x) = Ax) for all vectors (x) in (mathbb{R}^n). Matrix multiplication corresponds to the composition of linear maps. Ranks The rank of a matrix is the dimension of the image of the linear map it represents. It is also the dimension of the space spanned by its rows or columns. Alternatively, the rank can be defined as the smallest number (k) such that the matrix can be expressed as the product of an (m times k) matrix and a (k times n) matrix. Square Matrices and Related Definitions A square matrix has the same number of rows and columns. The set of all (n times n) square matrices forms a ring under matrix addition and multiplication. The identity matrix (I_n) is a square matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere. A square matrix (A) is invertible if there exists a matrix (B) such that (AB = BA = I_n). The determinant of a square matrix is a scalar value that can be used to determine whether the matrix is invertible. Special Types of Matrices Symmetric Matrices: These satisfy (A^T = A), where (A^T) is the transpose of (A). Skew-Symmetric Matrices: These satisfy (A^T = -A), and all diagonal elements are zero. Hermitian Matrices: These satisfy (A^H = A), where (A^H) is the conjugate transpose of (A). Toeplitz Matrices: These have constant values along each diagonal. Stochastic Matrices: These are square matrices where each row is a probability vector. Idempotent Matrices: These satisfy (A^2 = A). Applications 1. Encryption: Matrices can encrypt numerical data by multiplying a data matrix with a key matrix. Decryption involves multiplying the encrypted matrix by the inverse of the key matrix. 2. Computer Graphics: Transformation matrices, often (4 times 4), are used to manipulate 3D objects in computer graphics. History The study of matrices dates back to ancient times. The Chinese text The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art (300 BC–200 AD) used matrix methods to solve linear equations. The concept of determinants appeared in this text long before their formal development by Leibniz and Seki Kowa in the 17th century. The term matrix was introduced by J.J. Sylvester in 1848. Over time, mathematicians like Cayley, Hamilton, and von Neumann contributed significantly to matrix theory. Education Matrices are traditionally taught in linear algebra courses at the college level. In the United States, they have been included in high school curricula since the 1990s, often requiring the use of graphing calculators. Some programming languages and mathematical software are designed to handle matrix operations efficiently. Abstract Algebra Matrices over a ring or semiring can be studied in abstract algebra. The set of all (n times n) matrices over a commutative ring forms a unitary associative algebra. Determinants and invertibility can also be defined in this context. Matrices Without Entries Matrices with zero rows or columns, such as a (3 times 0) matrix, are valid in certain mathematical contexts, particularly in linear maps between vector spaces. These matrices have no entries but are defined by their dimensions.
